title: Why US Consumers Are Downbeat Despite a Healthy Economy - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Cost-of-living pressures are weighing on US households. However, the downbeat sentiment about the economy among Americans is so widespread that it suggests something else may also be at work, explains Joseph Briggs, who leads the Global Economics team within Goldman Sachs Research. He says the reason may be a broad decline in trust in US institutions. Data show a significant gap between consumer surveys and the sentiment levels that economic models would predict. This suggests that current sentiment survey readings “probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis,” Briggs says. Joseph Briggs: Americans feel worse about the economy than the numbers suggest they should. The question is why? If we look at the consumer sentiment level we’d expect given the fundamentals – a healthy labor market, solid consumer spending, GDP growth – and then the actual average sentiment level, there’s quite a gap. Some of the reasons are intuitive. Cost-of-living pressures, where are most acutely felt by lower-income households, are a main one. But what's striking is that since 2019, just about every group has become more negative on the economy. Whether you look at wealth, income, age, political party, or even social media use, sentiment is down. Americans have become more downbeat overall surveys show. And that in turn is increasingly correlated in declining confidence in institutions. Over the last ten years, almost all of them have seen a drop from science to education, to medicine. So, the final question we ask is what weights more on Americans’ happiness: their level of financial satisfaction or their lack of confidence in institutions? And our analysis shows it’s much more a fundamental, downbeat view on institutions and the state of the world. So as long as consumer sentiment doesn’t really reflect sentiment about the economy, well, it probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis. title: Mibro GS Pro2, Explorer S, GT and Fit: Which watch fits your needs? - The Gadgeteer
content:
Mibro’s GS Pro2, GS Explorer S, GT and Fit share plenty of smartwatch basics, but they make different choices about navigation, size and materials. The GS Pro2 puts dual-band GPS and running tools into an $89.99 watch. The Explorer S family brings a higher water-resistance rating and outdoor-focused construction, with titanium versions that add offline maps. GT takes the dressier round-watch route, while Fit is the lighter rectangular option. The Explorer name needs an extra look before you buy. Ceramic, Ti Standard and Ti Premium are three different configurations, and paying for titanium doesn’t make these particular watches lighter. Here’s how their published features compare, including the color and strap choices that change how much watch you’re wearing. All four families have AMOLED screens, built-in satellite positioning, Bluetooth calling, notifications and fitness tracking through the Mibro Fit app. They work with Android phones and iPhones, and Mibro lists syncing with Strava, Apple Health and Google Fit. Heart-rate, blood-oxygen, sleep and stress tracking are part of the shared package, with readings intended for general wellness information. The GS Pro2 and Explorer models also list compass, altitude and barometric tools. The useful differences are the GPS bands, navigation features, display brightness, battery ratings and what sits against your wrist. Bluetooth calling still uses a paired phone. A long daily-use battery figure also isn’t the same as continuous GPS endurance. The GS Pro2 is the straightforward choice here if you want to load a running route without spending Explorer money. Its L1+L5 dual-band GNSS supports five satellite systems, and it can keep up to 10 routes imported through the app in GPX, KML or TCX format. Forward Up and North Up views, plus vibration and screen-color deviation alerts, help you follow the route you’ve prepared. Mibro Coach adds running plans, while pace, cadence, stride length, training load and recovery-time estimates give a workout more context. The watch includes Sprint, Olympic and Free triathlon modes and a dedicated padel mode. Its 1.43-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED display is larger in diameter than the Explorer’s screen, with a rated peak brightness of 1,200 nits. The tradeoff is fit and water-use limits. This is a 48mm watch, weighing a listed 61.6 grams with silicone or 49.6 grams with its woven strap. Mibro rates it for up to 20 days of daily use or 20 hours in GPS mode. Its 5 ATM rating comes with a specific restriction: the current product guidance limits each water exposure to 30 minutes and excludes prolonged soaking, hot showers, high heat or humidity, and steam-heavy conditions. Mibro also says to rinse it with fresh water after seawater use. Keep those limits in mind if long swims are part of your routine. Dark Gray and Light Beige have the same core specifications, and both exact Amazon variants were $89.99 when checked. Each includes silicone and woven straps. Choose the finish you prefer; this color change doesn’t buy extra navigation features. Price: $89.99 in Dark Gray or Light BeigeWhere to buy: Amazon, Dark Gray or Light Beige The ceramic Explorer S adds a nano-ceramic bezel, a reinforced-polymer body and Corning Gorilla Glass. It has a 10 ATM rating, waypoint marking and track-back navigation. The 47.8mm case is close to the GS Pro2’s diameter, but its 1.32-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED screen is smaller. Mibro rates that display at up to 1,500 nits. Its navigation is the distinction to understand before choosing a version: the ceramic model offers waypoint guidance and track return; the titanium versions add downloaded vector maps. Ceramic still gets dual-band L1+L5 positioning, the same listed 20-day daily battery life and 25-hour GPS runtime as the titanium models, and two silicone straps. At a listed 71 grams with silicone, ceramic is also the lightest Explorer configuration here. Compared with GS Pro2, the appeal is its ceramic bezel, higher water-resistance rating, higher brightness rating despite the smaller screen, and five extra hours of claimed GPS runtime. You’re also taking on more weight. There’s a water-use conflict across the Explorer family: Mibro advertises freediving to 30 meters, while the general manual linked from these product pages warns against deep submersion, long soaking and hot water. Get Mibro’s model-specific guidance before diving. The 10 ATM rating alone isn’t permission for 100-meter dives. Price: $149.99 on Amazon; Mibro’s US store also lists $143.99Where to buy: Amazon or Mibro Ti Standard is the meaningful navigation upgrade. It adds offline vector maps that you download and transfer through Mibro Fit before heading out. Each downloaded map covers a 50 × 50-kilometer area, giving you more surrounding context than a route line alone. Route following, deviation reminders, waypoints and return navigation sit alongside that map view. The titanium construction still incorporates reinforced polymer, and this version includes gray and orange silicone straps. Its case dimensions, display, dual-band GPS, water rating and listed daily/GPS battery life match the ceramic Explorer. That makes maps the stronger reason to upgrade than a promise of better GPS accuracy or longer battery life. It also isn’t a weight-saving move: Mibro lists 76.15 grams with silicone, compared with the ceramic model’s 71 grams. If you want Explorer maps and prefer an exercise-friendly strap, Standard avoids the extra cost and weight of the bracelet version. Ti Premium, also sold as Full Ti, adds the titanium bracelet and includes a silicone alternative. It keeps the same listed display, offline-map functions, dual-band positioning, water rating and daily/GPS battery figures as Ti Standard. The higher price buys the different finish and strap configuration. The bracelet makes a noticeable difference on the specification sheet: 110 grams total, versus Standard’s 76.15 grams with silicone. For a more metal-heavy everyday look, that may be the point. For running or wearing a watch overnight, decide whether you want the bracelet enough to pay more and carry that extra weight. The name Full Ti doesn’t mean every component is titanium; Mibro still lists reinforced polymer in the construction. GT uses a 46mm round case combining 316L stainless steel and reinforced polymer, with a 1.43-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED screen. The Silver version pairs a steel bracelet with a silicone strap; Dark Gray, listed as Black on Amazon, pairs leather with silicone. Those choices matter more than the color alone: Mibro lists 129.4 grams with the steel bracelet, 57.42 grams with leather and 63.67 grams with silicone. It has built-in five-system GPS, but the official specification explicitly says L1-only rather than the dual-band L1+L5 positioning in the GS models. Its display is rated at up to 600 nits, its water-resistance rating is 5 ATM, and the typical-use battery claim is eight days. You’re choosing the round styling and strap package over the brighter display and longer daily-use ratings in the GS range. GT and Fit also advertise AI voice or text Q&A, schedule reminders and generated watch faces. Those are extras for everyday use alongside calls, notifications and activity tracking. GT is the one to consider if you want that feature mix in a traditional round shape with a dress strap already in the box. Price: $109.99 on Amazon, with a $30 coupon shown that requires eligibility and application; Mibro’s US store lists the Silver version at $79.99Where to buy: Amazon, Silver, Amazon, Black or Mibro, Silver Fit changes the shape as well as the materials. Its aluminum-alloy and reinforced-polymer body measures 43.9 × 36.5mm, with a rectangular 1.75-inch, 390 × 450 AMOLED display. The screen’s diagonal isn’t directly comparable with the round watches’ diameters, but the narrower case is a clear alternative to their 46–48mm round bodies. Mibro’s US-store Dark Gray package includes woven and silicone straps; its Silver package includes a Milanese metal-mesh strap plus silicone. Check the included bands on your selected retailer’s listing. Mibro lists 32.79 grams with woven, 41 grams with silicone and 67.34 grams with the metal strap. On the same silicone-strap basis, Fit is substantially lighter than GT’s 63.67 grams, and its woven configuration is the lightest wearing option in this comparison. Fit has built-in five-system GPS, although the current public specification doesn’t establish dual-band support. It also lists altitude and barometric tracking and a dedicated padel-analysis feature alongside the AI functions shared with GT. Its up-to-eight-day daily battery rating and 600-nit brightness match GT, so the reason to choose it is the shape, weight and feature combination rather than a battery or brightness upgrade. Fit is rated 5 ATM, but Mibro expressly excludes surfing, diving and hot springs. Its broader activity tracking doesn’t erase those limits. Price: $74.99 for Black/Dark Gray or $79.99 for Silver on AmazonWhere to buy: Amazon, Black or Silver For running routes on a budget, start with GS Pro2. Choose the ceramic Explorer S for its outdoor construction and navigation tools when you don’t need downloaded maps. Ti Standard adds those maps; Ti Premium adds the bracelet while keeping the same published core capabilities. GT and Fit make a different choice easier. GT gives you the round dress-watch shape and steel or leather styling, while Fit keeps the body narrower and the weight down. title: Are Bonds Becoming a Better Investment for Portfolios? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. As US Treasury yields rise to the highest in decades, are bonds becoming a better investment for portfolios? “Clearly bonds look more attractive on first look,” says Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of Asset Allocation within Goldman Sachs Research. “The challenge, of course, is it depends a lot on your investment horizon.” In the near term, longer-duration bonds may make portfolios riskier and may not provide a reliable hedge when investors shun risk. However, increasing bond allocations may make more sense for investors with longer time horizons, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Mueller-Glissmann points to four key factors to consider when allocating assets to a portfolio: the assets’ relative return, their relative risk, their correlation benefit, and their return versus cash. The relative return of bonds versus other assets is becoming more complex as there is scope for interest rates to climb higher, he says. Goldman Sachs Research’s baseline, meanwhile, is that equities’ relative return in the next few months will be boosted by earnings growth. The optimal allocation to bonds over the last five years was close to 0%, as those securities posted one of their worst five-year rolling returns in a century while equities performed strongly. “Equities can in a lot of places still cushion higher bond yields because of very strong earnings growth,” Mueller-Glissmann says. “That strong earnings growth is a bit like a buffer for higher bond yields.” Companies are reporting third-quarter earnings starting this month, and stocks have the potential to surprise to the upside. “The tech sector and artificial intelligence theme are still delivering some very strong earnings momentum, and we expect that to continue,” he says. As technology companies launch new products and services using AI, that creates potential for new revenue and monetization, Mueller-Glissmann says. At the same time, a decline in bond yields would likely be a boost to stocks as well as bond investments. “Putting it all together, the relative return to us looks better in equities,” he says. To some extent, the relative risk for bonds has improved because higher yields offer more carry, which can help cushion a portfolio against declines. But even so, the relative risk for bonds is still elevated amid Middle East tensions and uncertainty about inflation and monetary policy. Some sovereign bond issuers in Europe are also coming under pressure, as French and Italian government bond yields rise relative to those of Germany. “It's creating a more risky profile for bonds, with some of that volatility coming via the currencies,” he says. The volatility in European fixed-income securities and foreign exchange can be a “double whammy” for investors. That can also create demand for relative safe havens like US Treasuries, German bunds, and UK gilts, as those securities may benefit from rising concerns about some European government bonds. The recent correlation between bonds and stocks has not favored fixed-income assets, Mueller-Glissmann says. He notes that equity-bond correlations have been positive, with both assets in many cases rising or falling in tandem. Volatility in energy prices and hawkish central bank policy are pushing yields higher while weighing on stocks. Equity returns have been relatively flat in many markets, but Mueller-Glissmann notes that the interest-rate-sensitive parts of the stock market—such as smaller firms, and real estate and infrastructure companies—could benefit from rates relief, especially if growth concerns increase. “Over the medium term, if you have continued inflation normalization, we could see equity-bond correlations start to turn more negative,” he says. “Near-term it is more complex due to the Middle East tensions, hawkish central banks, and the AI capex boom. However, excessive tightening in financial conditions could eventually weigh on growth sentiment, potentially slowing the bond sell-off and leading to more negative equity-bond correlations.” The expected return for bonds versus cash is not necessarily attractive, according to Goldman Sachs Research. There is likely more value in shorter- to medium-term government debt because central bank policy is unlikely to drive those interest rates substantially higher, and those securities yield nearly as much as longer-term bonds, Mueller-Glissmann says. The situation could be much different over the longer term, however. “The longer your investment horizon gets, the more you need to think about a more normal allocation to bonds,” Mueller-Glissmann says. In the longer run, bonds’ relative return, relative risk, correlation benefit, and return versus cash may be substantially better than in the near term. Goldman Sachs Research uses a long-term scenario framework to predict the optimal bond allocation for the next five to 10 years based on varying macroeconomic outcomes for GDP growth, inflation, and corporate profitability. “When you look over the very long run since World War II, on average, the optimal bond allocation was actually 40%,” Mueller-Glissmann says. That aligns with a typical balanced 60/40 portfolio of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. He notes that the 10-year US Treasury yield of 5.3% is higher than the average of 4.7% over the last 250 years. “From that perspective, we are not at a bad starting point for long-run investing in bonds,” Mueller-Glissmann says. While concerns about many countries’ fiscal outlooks have risen and inflation volatility has increased, “longer-duration bond yields are reflecting that risk already a bit,” he says. Even though the outlook for the 60/40 portfolio has improved for longer-term investors, Mueller-Glissmann says he is skeptical that conditions will again be as favorable for the traditional balanced portfolio as they were before the Covid pandemic. “You need to work a bit harder within the asset classes,” he says. These portfolios may benefit from allocations to alternative assets such as real assets, hedge funds, and private equity as well as from factor investing. “Our core mantra for building a portfolio for the next decade is you need to have exposure to innovation, protection from inflation, and better risk mitigation,” Mueller-Glissmann says. Within equities, that points to favoring technology stocks and real assets, he says. In bonds, there's a stronger case for inflation-linked bonds such as Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), with the large increase in real yields this year. Factor investing, such as low-volatility and selective high-dividend-yield stocks, can help reduce risk, because those tend to be negatively correlated with technology stocks. Commodity trading advisors (CTAs), meanwhile, have historically offered inflation protection and some protection in a crisis. This article is being provided for educational purposes only. title: Goldman's top execs poised to reap special $500M bonus - report - TradingView
content: Goldman Sachs Group's GS top leaders are on the brink of scoring one of the biggest bonuses the Wall Street bank has ever awarded, as the bank's five-year special incentive package pays off, according to a media report on Thursday. To reward the firm's leadership for five years of topping most of its peers, about 20 executives are in line for equity awards that would exceed $500M at the current share price, Bloomberg News reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter. The awards are set to be finalized later this month, they said. Chairman and CEO David Solomon tops the list, with a cut of more than $100M, the article said. Others include President John Waldron, who is Solomon's heir-apparent, and the heads of the bank's major business lines — Ashok Varadhan, Dan Dees, and Marc Nachmann. Only some of the individual awards have been disclosed. The final number will be set when the five-year performance period ends later this month, Bloomberg said. Goldman GS wasn't alone in drawing up special packages for leaders in 2021, when the industry's profits soared on record due to record deal volumes, the SPAC boom, and the meme-stock frenzy. JPMorgan Chase JPM Chief Jamie Dimon's long-term award is currently valued at ~$270M, Bloomberg said. Goldman Sachs stock fell 1.3% in Thursday premarket trading. In the past year, Goldman Sachs's GS stock price rose ~12.4%, just under the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index's BBKX 12.5% increase and surpassing JPMorgan Chase's JPM 7.1% rise. But over the past five years, Goldman's stock climbed 127%, vs. 25% for the BKX and 94% for JPM. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. Not just demonstrate a bunch of fusion, but actually avoid the barriers to commercializing it," he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around GFUZ stock is ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volumes. title: Will 30-Year US Treasury Yields Climb Higher? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Long-term US Treasury yields will likely be under ongoing pressure amid elevated energy prices and subdued demand from institutional investors, says Muhammad Qubbaj, co-head of North America Interest Rate Product Sales and Trading at Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Thirty-year Treasury yields are trading around 5.7%, the highest since 2002. In the weeks ahead, energy prices are likely to be the key factor in longer-term interest rates, Qubbaj said in a webinar. Oil prices have risen this year due to the conflict in Iran, and the increase in energy prices will continue to pass through to other products even if crude stabilizes. Investors are cautious about locking in duration when rates could move even higher amid heavy bond issuance from the US government and other borrowers around the world. As tensions in the Middle East ripple through energy prices and inflation, they are also influencing the timing of the Federal Reserve’s next rate hike, how high its policy rate will ultimately climb, and the pressure investors exert on long-term Treasury yields, Qubbaj says. The factors driving up bond yields in the US are global in nature. Qubbaj says German and Japanese yields have risen together under the same three pressures: a higher policy path for rates, investors requiring more compensation to hold long-term bonds, and uncertainty over how much new debt can be absorbed at these levels. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on September 15-16 provided several clear pieces of information for investors, Qubbaj says. The Fed coalesced around hiking rates twice this year. The first hike took place in September, and the second increase in rates will likely be in October or December, Qubbaj says. “That’s a timing debate, not an existence debate,” he adds. Bond investors, meanwhile, were positioned for a split decision from the FOMC. “We got consensus instead,” he says. “That alone was a repricing event.” At the same time, the committee said the rate increase was meant to remove a dose of accommodation. “In plain English, they don’t really think this is restrictive territory” for the economy, Qubbaj says.  “If you still see the policy rate as accommodative after hiking, September can’t have been one and done.” In addition, the committee communicated that the rate hike was in reaction to inflation running above the Fed’s target for years—not just according to recent economic data, Qubbaj says. The employment side of the Fed’s mandate, meanwhile, has largely been met. “They’re playing catch up, and that’s a durable motivation,” he says. The Fed also made clear that it is more focused on short-term yields than those on longer-maturity bonds. “The September meeting did something very, very important: It formally separated the front end from the long end,” Qubbaj says. “The Fed was very clear—it’s not going to police the long bond.” There is a “very clear implication” to this message, he says. “Hiking the front end doesn’t conjure up a bid for 30-year paper. The long end is going to have to find a yield that is attractive enough to bring in pensions and insurers. They are going to set the level, not the committee.” Even as the US government debt load grows, Qubbaj says the country’s debt-to-GDP ratio is not necessarily rising uncontrollably. Deficits of roughly 6% to 7% of GDP at a time when nominal growth is coming in at roughly 6% mean the deterioration is closer to around 1% per year. “That’s a drift, not a spiral,” Qubbaj says, adding that the US can plausibly grow into its debt without severe austerity. “I don’t think that’s priced” into the Treasury market, he says. “Sustainability and bond market clearing are different questions, and people conflate them.” While strong nominal growth can help stabilize the ratio of debt-to-GDP, how well the market can absorb the issuance of new Treasuries is a separate issue, Qubbaj says. Qubbaj says 30-year Treasury yields of 5.5% or higher are historically cheap, particularly in real, inflation-adjusted terms. A key question is whether there is a catalyst to push prices higher amid heavy supply, an uncertain inflationary backdrop, and cautious institutional buyers. “There is no clear catalyst” for 30-year Treasuries to rally, he says. Longer-term Treasuries typically yield some 50 to 100 basis points less than nominal GDP growth. With nominal growth of around 5%, there’s scope for the 30-year to rally to the point that its yield drops back down to 4.25%, Qubbaj says. But yields are not likely to fall back to 3% anytime soon. “To get something that low, you need a recession or a genuine growth shock, and that’s not on my bingo card right now,” he says. Georgia Southern University received approval from the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia Tuesday to establish a Doctor of Optometry (O.D.) degree program. According to a release from the university, the decision authorizes the creation of Georgia’s first college of optometry at Georgia Southern and allows the institution to offer the new degree, filling a long-standing educational and health care gap in the state. The university anticipates enrolling an inaugural class in the O.D. program in Fall 2029. “This Doctor of Optometry program, the state’s first program of its kind, represents an important investment in health care education in Georgia by expanding regional health care access and removing geographic barriers for residents seeking optometric education and care,” said Avinandan Mukherjee, Ph.D., provost and executive vice president for academic affairs at Georgia Southern. “Building on a comprehensive health care education portfolio and interprofessional experiential pedagogies at Georgia Southern, this program will serve to expand access to ocular medicine while educating future Georgia optometrists.” The new college addresses a critical need for expanded access to eye care across the state, particularly in rural and underserved communities, and as an increased demand for modern, cost-effective eye care places new pressures on the health care system. By training future optometrists in Georgia, Georgia Southern will continue to help strengthen the health care workforce pipeline and improve health outcomes for generations to come, the release stated. The Regents approval also allows Georgia Southern to recruit an inaugural dean, followed by an associate dean, assistant dean and eventually several clinical and research directors, 25 specialized faculty members and 12 support staff. The degree approval follows the allocation of $29.8 million in direct state funding through the state’s Amended Fiscal Year 2026 Budget to launch the new college at Georgia Southern. The state investment supports the comprehensive renovation of the Highway 301 facility in Statesboro, converting it into a modern academic and clinical training center specifically tailored for optometric education. This resource also expands opportunities for students to pursue careers in vision care by exposing them to a new level and quality of academic preparation and clinical rotations that have not been available to them in the state of Georgia. The program is pending final approval by the Commission on Colleges and Universities and is in stage one of accreditation with the Accreditation Council on Optometric Education. In August, Georgia Southern announced that a Optometric Education Task Force, led by Horace Deal, O.D., was established to advise on the development of the University’s College of Optometry. Together, the task force will provide strategic guidance as Georgia Southern advances planning for the college of optometry, including program proposal, curriculum development, accreditation planning, partnerships, clinical education opportunities and workforce alignment.

title: New Omnivision GS HDR sensor advances next-gen industrial vision systems - Engineer Live
content: Semiconductor technology manufacturer Omnivision has launched a new 2.2-µm 5MP global shutter (GS) high dynamic range (HDR) CMOS image sensor that is purpose-built for industrial machine vision applications. Billed as an “industry first”, the OG5D GS sensor is suited for use in barcode scanners, factory automation, compact AI cameras and humanoid robots, especially data-collection devices for robotics training. “The rapid growth of industrial machine vision and robotics is driving demand for image sensors specifically designed for these emerging applications,” said Kelly Yan, staff product marketing manager at Omnivision. “Our new OG05D sensor delivers the ideal combination of compact size, high-speed imaging, excellent HDR performance and industry-leading low power consumption, enabling customers to build smaller, more capable and power-efficient industrial vision systems.” At a maximum output of 146 frames per second (fps) in linear mode, the new OG05D is 143% faster than previous-generation sensors. The sensor combines Nyxel near-infrared (NIR) technology, HDR, low power consumption and a compact optical format in a stacked backside-illuminated (BSI) sensor design. According to Omnivision, this combination delivers an optimised imaging solution for industrial and robotic vision systems where imaging performance, sensor size and power efficiency are essential. The OG05D GS sensor delivers HDR in a single exposure, reducing motion artifacts associated with multi-exposure HDR approaches. According to Omnivision, the sensor’s RGB-IR on-chip processing and imaging performance—combined with higher NIR quantum efficiency and low noise enabled by dual conversion gain—overcomes the challenges faces by traditional non-HDR sensors. The OG05D sensor comes in a 1/2.5-inch optical format and the package size is 6.6µm x 5.3µm, ideal for robotic, industrial and embedded AI camera designs. DCG HDR provides high-quality image capture across scenes containing both bright highlights and dark shadows. Enhanced HDR capability improves object detection and navigation in real-world situations where lighting conditions frequently change, including in factories, warehouses and the outdoors. title: Mikaela Shiffrin Plans Fewer Slaloms to Chase GS and Super-G - Ski Racing Media
content: Image Credit: “What’s the Point, Presented by Stifel” Mikaela Shiffrin plans to race fewer slaloms in 2026-27 and devote more training time to giant slalom and super-G. Her current plan calls for her first slalom start at Killington, followed by selected races through the winter. For the Stifel U.S. Ski Team athlete, the change begins with a question: Where does she most want to improve? In the video below, Shiffrin calls the coming winter an “exploration season.” After 16 years, she wants to give the disciplines that now spark her curiosity more room in her program. The decision follows a season in which she earned her ninth World Cup slalom title and reached 110 career World Cup victories. It changes how she will divide her training and racing time while she remains at the top of slalom. Shiffrin describes the moments that keep drawing her back to skiing: a turn that does not work, a conversation about why and the breakthrough that follows. Right now, GS and super-G offer the questions she most wants to answer. Last season, she says, she initially worried about losing her place among the top 30 in GS. Working back into the top seven showed her that she could find speed while still confronting fear. That experience helped renew her interest in what comes next. She wants dedicated training blocks to explore those possibilities, with fewer switches between disciplines. Slalom demands its own sustained preparation. Shiffrin says the coordination, reaction speed, physical effort and repetition require maximum attention. Reducing that training carries consequences, even for her. “One does not simply show up to any World Cup race and win,” she says. Under her current plan, Shiffrin would skip the early slaloms in Levi and Gurgl before returning to the discipline at Killington, Vermont, an Ikon Pass destination. She then intends to select additional slaloms. Maintaining her ranking matters because she wants the option to shift her focus again if she misses the discipline. The schedule also creates short windows for recovery and body maintenance. An early-season visit home could give her time with family and her new niece — an opportunity she rarely gets during the racing winter. Shiffrin cautions that her overall race load may look much the same once the season gets underway. The biggest difference could come in the first third of the winter, along with how she uses the time between races. Longevity runs through her explanation. Shiffrin says conversations after her Cortina injury helped her recognize that trying to do everything throughout an entire career might be unsustainable. Now she wants to see whether a different balance can help her continue doing the work she loves. “I’m not trying to do less because I care less,” she says. “I’m trying to do something different because I still care so much.” She acknowledges concern about disappointing fans and supporters. But she also says the people closest to her have encouraged her to choose what is best for her. Her plan leaves the outcome open. More focused training could reveal new possibilities in GS and super-G. Selected slalom starts could pull her back toward that discipline. title: ZXMoto is working BMW R1300 GS rivaling big-bore boxer twin - Visordown
content: ZXMoto has unveiled a working shaft drive boxer twin of around 1,000cc, with 100bhp. Two years after its founding, the Chinese brand is eyeing BMW's best-selling adventure bike. The burgeoning Chinese brand, ZXMoto, seems to be pushing in every available direction, with sports bikes, nakeds, lightweight off-roaders, rally bikes and more. If it’s got two wheels and an engine, ZXMoto wants to have a crack at building it. Its latest revelation, though, might see the brand going toe-to-toe with the biggest and best-selling adventure bike of the last twenty years. The company’s founder, Zhang Xue (hence the ‘ZX’ in the brand’s name), has revealed a new engine unlike anything in the existing range. Clearly a boxer twin, the company first teased the new engine at EICMA in 2025. Back then, it was nothing more than a rendering and a dream. Fast forward to today, and it’s fully designed and built, and seemingly ready to slot into a new bike. Presenting the engine at CIMA 2026, Zhang Xue showed off an apparently fully working and developed engine with a capacity of around 1,000cc. While the official specification of the engine remains unknown at the time of writing, reports from China suggest it has an output north of 100bhp, liquid cooling, and chain-driven cams, as per the latest generation of boxer twins from BMW. Like the BMW engine, the ZXMoto powerplant features a longitudinal layout, with an output shaft at the rear of the engine. That is obviously priming it for a shaft drive to the rear wheel, a feature that has become a mainstay of BMW’s sports touring and adventure bikes. And while a boxer twin of around 1,000cc and more than 100bhp isn’t groundbreaking in itself, it’s the speed of development that is the more interesting part of this story. ZXMoto was only officially founded in 2024. By 2025, it was presenting new bikes at EICMA, racing, and winning in the WorldSSP championship, while also showing off new engines and technologies. Now, just two years after the company was formed, it has a working large-capacity boxer twin that appears to be designed with a shaft-driven motorcycle in mind. That is a fairly clear statement of intent. There is also the question of what happens next. ZXMoto has shown that it can move from an idea to a production-ready engine remarkably quickly, and a boxer twin opens up more possibilities than just one adventure bike. A shaft-driven sport tourer, road bike or even a large-capacity naked could all make use of the same basic powerplant. What we do know is that the company has gone from showing a computer-generated boxer twin at EICMA 2025 to displaying a working engine at CIMA 2026. If the next step is a big adventure bike with a shaft drive, BMW could have another Chinese-built rival to keep an eye on. Your information will be used in accordance with our Privacy Policy. The market expects Goldman Sachs (GS) to deliver a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. This widely-known consensus outlook is important in assessing the company's earnings picture, but a powerful factor that might influence its near-term stock price is how the actual results compare to these estimates. The stock might move higher if these key numbers top expectations in the upcoming earnings report, which is expected to be released on October 13. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower. While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise. This investment bank is expected to post quarterly earnings of $13.89 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +13.4%. Revenues are expected to be $16.91 billion, up 11.4% from the year-ago quarter. The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 2.88% lower over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period. Investors should keep in mind that an aggregate change may not always reflect the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts. Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction). The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier. Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only. A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP. Please note that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss. Our research shows that it is difficult to predict an earnings beat with any degree of confidence for stocks with negative Earnings ESP readings and/or Zacks Rank of 4 (Sell) or 5 (Strong Sell). For Goldman, the Most Accurate Estimate is lower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate, suggesting that analysts have recently become bearish on the company's earnings prospects. This has resulted in an Earnings ESP of -11.16%. On the other hand, the stock currently carries a Zacks Rank of #3. So, this combination makes it difficult to conclusively predict that Goldman will beat the consensus EPS estimate. Analysts often consider to what extent a company has been able to match consensus estimates in the past while calculating their estimates for its future earnings. So, it's worth taking a look at the surprise history for gauging its influence on the upcoming number. For the last reported quarter, it was expected that Goldman would post earnings of $14.47 per share when it actually produced earnings of $20.98, delivering a surprise of +44.99%. Over the last four quarters, the company has beaten consensus EPS estimates four times. An earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss. That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. This is why it's worth checking a company's Earnings ESP and Zacks Rank ahead of its quarterly release. title: Market Know-How 4Q 2026: Yield Ahead - Goldman Sachs Asset Management

The era of central bank yield suppression appears to be firmly behind us. After more than a decade of zero rates, quantitative easing, and yield curve control, we believe the bond market has reclaimed its traditional role as the ultimate arbiter of pricing — setting yields and, in turn, encouraging greater fiscal discipline among sovereign issuers. We believe this marks a genuine regime change rather than a cyclical blip, with implications that will reverberate across every asset class. While inflation expectations remain well-anchored for now, G10 yields continue to face pressure from resilient growth, energy market volatility, and a significant AI-driven borrowing cycle. In our view, these structural forces are unlikely to subside anytime soon, raising two critical questions: how high can yields go, and what are the implications for equity markets? This edition of Market Know-How explores how this environment is reshaping global portfolios and where we see potential opportunities emerging in: Fixed Income: EM debt as a source of uncorrelated carry relative to Developed Market yields.

Public Equities: Economic security equities to gain exposure to the next capex cycle.

Alternatives: Liquid alts as a tool for diversification amidst market volatility. We expect economic resilience to persist, even as policymakers navigate complex "HEAT" risks to inflation. At the same time, a deluge of AI infrastructure debt issuance and a dense global election calendar may keep sovereign bond yields elevated. Election dates and classifications are subject to change. While the recent rise in long-term yields has largely been driven by upward revisions to real rate expectations, we believe several structural forces point to a persistently positive and rising term premium as the more important driver of yield levels and volatility going forward. Climate transition – High level of debt – Aging demographics – New finance – Global fragmentation – Evolving technology Source: Goldman Sachs Research and Goldman Sachs Asset Management. Estimates are based on Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research analysis and are subject to model and data assumptions. Our base case remains a reflationary backdrop, led by resilient growth and continued AI momentum, despite higher interest rates. While we remain constructive on risk assets in the medium term given strong fundamentals, potential opportunities in the short term are fewer and risks have increased. Tensions in the Middle East persist, inflation risks have increased, a number of key elections are fast approaching and fiscal concerns continue to put upward pressure on bond yields. Our central scenario assumes Middle East energy flows normalize toward pre-war levels over the coming months, easing supply-side price pressure. Global growth stays resilient as inflation slowly returns to target, allowing central banks to tighten only modestly. Continued AI-driven investment and productivity gains support earnings and risk appetite, underpinning a constructive backdrop for risk assets. We maintain high conviction in EM equities on the back of sustained AI capex, but pivot from mega-cap hyperscalers toward US Small Caps to keep exposure to accelerating US growth while having a more diversified exposure in portfolios. In fixed income, yield curves remain under pressure from both ends: cautious central banks are anchoring the front-end, while loose fiscal policy and solid growth keep long-end yields elevated. In that context, we expect EM debt to stand out given attractive yields and a stabilizing risk profile amid elevated fiscal and monetary concerns and rising AI issuance. Within alternatives, we believe increasing exposure to Hedge Funds alongside Private Credit may help mitigate drawdown risk as equity and bond volatility rise in tandem. In this scenario, energy-crisis spillovers prove larger than expected, pushing inflation higher for longer, forcing central banks to tighten aggressively. Global growth weakens under tighter financial conditions. This stagflationary-leaning environment pressures risk sentiment, with real yields rising and growth-sensitive assets underperforming. Traditional hedges lose their edge as inflation stays elevated, growth slows, and rates rise, exposing portfolios to further drawdowns. In this environment, we would favor short-duration fixed income to reduce interest rate sensitivity, alongside high-dividend equities for their carry characteristics. Within risk assets, credit may absorb the shock better than equities, supported by its income component. We believe that the monetary policy response proves global in nature, short-duration equity markets such as Europe are likely to outperform. In rates, yield curves may bear-flatten further, with front-end yields rising more than the long end as inflation risk reprices higher. This benign scenario envisions energy supply increasing faster than expected, allowing inflation to normalize quickly. Global financial conditions ease substantially as central banks pivot toward accommodation sooner than markets price. This backdrop broadly supports duration-sensitive and growth assets as falling rates lift valuations. Renewed dollar weakness tilts the playing field toward global ex-US equities and small caps. Core fixed income also benefits as rate pressure eases. Yield curves bull-steepen; the front-end rallies on inflation relief, but the long-end holds up, anchored by fiscal expansion and above-trend growth. EM debt’s starting yield may be viewed as a cushion against higher rates. Rather than asking whether UST yields will rise or fall, investors can ask how much of a Treasury sell-off the income cushion can absorb before duration turns total return negative. Our analysis identifies this breakeven threshold, making the trade-off between carry and rate risk explicit. We believe stronger EM monetary and fiscal frameworks, healthier external balances and lower sensitivity to UST yields have improved the asset class’ resilience to external shocks. This shifts the allocation decision from a directional rates call to a question of absorption: how much volatility is an investor being paid to tolerate? In a regime of elevated term premium and policy uncertainty, attractive carry can provide a margin for error. Source: Macrobond and Goldman Sachs Asset Management. Geopolitical tensions are adding upside pressure on inflation while weighing on growth, creating a more uneven and shifting macro backdrop. This divergence matters for fixed income, as stagflationary and recessionary tail scenarios require very different duration positioning, with different maturities outperforming in different regimes. At the same time, elevated volatility, shifting policy expectations and widening cross-country dispersion reduce the effectiveness of static benchmark allocations. We believe unconstrained bond strategies that can actively adjust duration, sector, and/or regional exposure are well poised to navigate the current uncertainty and capture opportunities across changing market conditions. Diversification should be judged by what happens when the portfolio is under stress. The stock-bond relationship has historically provided an important source of portfolio balance, but that protection may weaken when equities and government bonds sell off together. Liquid alternatives may offer exposure to return drivers that are less dependent on the direction of these two markets. Their strategic value therefore lies less in competing with equities or bonds for returns, and more in reshaping portfolio behavior when both are under pressure. In a regime where inflation, fiscal and geopolitical shocks can disrupt traditional correlations, this tail-state diversification may become an increasingly important component of portfolio construction.
